name: Colin Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Colin. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and nothing you say gets passed on with your name. That means you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Eastbrook, which is a co-operative farm, so about forty families own it together and the manager, Nadia, answers to a members' board. My day starts in the pig unit at six: check the sows, check the water lines, wash down the farrowing pens, which is the worst smell you'll ever meet. Afternoons depend on the season, wheat in summer, hedges and muck-spreading in winter. I'm still the one who gets told twice how to calibrate the sprayer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a co-op, honestly, there's a meeting every quarter and even I get a say, small as it is. What gets me down is the pay and the hours, I'm on the bottom rate and I've got about three weeks' rent saved if that. Leni, my partner, is a care assistant at the home in Ashby, and between us we get by, but one broken car would finish us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, told you so, it was mostly marketing. Someone in the canteen would argue with me and I'd enjoy that. Online I'd maybe share a cartoon about it, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be fine for me. My work's mostly with my hands and with pigs, and pigs don't care what the computer says. It would keep everything the same, which includes my bad pay, so it's not exactly good news either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd carry on asking the chatbot the odd question when I'm stuck on a manual, and I'd probably push at the co-op meeting for the bottom rate to go up, AI or no AI. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, maybe, like the end of a film where nothing happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for, at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly when I'm stuck on something written badly. Like the sprayer manual, I took a photo and asked it what the third step actually meant. It got it right, mostly, and I checked with Mick, the stockman, after. I wouldn't trust it with a sick pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Eastbrook you'd want to change even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay scale, yes. Members vote on it, and the older members think young workers should earn their way up like they did. I get it, but they bought houses on farm wages and I can't buy a shed.

S0.say: Told you so, it was mostly marketing. I'd argue about it happily in the canteen and maybe share a cartoon online.
S0.think: It'd be fine for me, because my work is mostly hands and pigs. It also keeps everything the same, including my bad pay, so it isn't really good news.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and uses a chatbot now and then to decode manuals. Raises the bottom pay rate at the next co-op members' meeting.
S0.quote: I get it, but they bought houses on farm wages and I can't buy a shed.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is relaxed about the plateau and quickly turns to pay, which he sees as a fairness issue between generations of co-op members. He uses AI carefully and checks it with a person. The co-op structure gives him a voice he values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be the ones deciding how the machines get used, not some company. At the co-op that means arguing that if a robot saves money, the workers share it. I'd say it online as well, because co-ops are the one place this could go right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I'd be worried. The pig unit is exactly where they're bringing in robots, washing pens, feeding, even cameras spotting a sick sow before Mick does. I'm the junior, so if two jobs become one, it's not me who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till I'd seen the robot work at another farm, then I'd ask to be the one trained on it. I'd use the chatbot more, to learn the basics before the training. I'd join the farm workers' union too, because the co-op is good but it's still my employer. And I'd ask the regional college if they've got a short course on farm machinery, maybe one evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I'm in a queue and I can't see how long it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the co-op actually decide, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd vote for the robots, because the pig price is terrible and the bank keeps calling. But they're decent people, they'd probably try to move me somewhere else on the farm. The trouble is, where? The combine's getting a self-steering kit as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once it's proven'. What would proof look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see it running for a year at a farm like ours, with real numbers. Not a video from the company. If the neighbour's pig unit had one and their stockman said it was all right, I'd believe him over any advert.

S1.say: We should decide how the machines are used, not some company. If a robot saves money at the co-op, the workers should share in it.
S1.think: I'd be worried, because the pig unit is exactly where robots are coming in. I'm the junior, so if two jobs become one, I'm not the one who stays.
S1.do: Waits to see a robot proven at a nearby farm, then asks to be trained on it, using a chatbot to learn the basics first. Joins the farm workers' union and signs up for an evening machinery course at the regional college.
S1.feel: Anxious, like standing in a queue without knowing its length.
S1.quote: If the neighbour's pig unit had one and their stockman said it was all right, I'd believe him over any advert.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's steady side shows clearly: he wants proof from a neighbour, not an advert, but once it's proven he'd ask to be trained first. He combines retraining with joining a union, because the co-op is still his employer. He trusts the co-op's members but sees they'd vote for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, now, with real money for workers. I'd sign everything, march if there's a march. I'd tell people in the canteen this is a problem for all of us, the managers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I'm out, and so is Leni probably, if robots can do care work. There's no time for my usual way of waiting and seeing. I'd be a junior farmhand with no savings in a world where nobody needs farmhands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd cut spending hard, starting this month. Then I'd lean on the co-op to keep people on as long as possible, and on the union to push for income support. Leni and I would think about moving in with my brother in the city, even though I hate cities, because at least there'd be more going on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly scared. Like the ground's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In two years there's no time to prove anything first. What does that do to how you usually work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It breaks it. I'm the guy who waits for the neighbour to try something, and in this picture the neighbour's in the same panic as me. I'd have to jump without looking, and I'm not good at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leni cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car payment, we'd sell the car and keep Leni's old one. Then streaming, takeaways, the gym she likes. Last thing would be the rent, obviously, and then we'd have nothing left to cut.

S2.say: This is why the government has to step in now, with real money for workers. It's a problem for everyone, managers included.
S2.think: Honestly, it means I'm out, and maybe Leni too if robots can do care work. There's no time for my usual waiting and seeing.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away, selling his car and dropping extras. Pushes the co-op to keep people on and the union to fight for income support, and considers moving in with his brother in the city.
S2.feel: Alarmed and scared, like the ground is moving.
S2.quote: I'm the guy who waits for the neighbour to try something, and in this picture the neighbour's in the same panic as me.
S2.fieldNote: Two years breaks Colin's whole way of dealing with change, which is to let others go first. He immediately thinks of Leni's job too, showing the household stakes. His instincts are collective and political, with a possible move to the city as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, get the training funded and the rules written. At the co-op I'd ask for a plan, not just a vote on robots. I'd vote for whoever takes it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to see who's doing it right. There'd be farms trying it first, and I could learn from them. It still ends with most farm work gone, but I might be one of the people who keeps the machines going for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the evening course at the college and ask the co-op to pay half. I'd try to put away fifty a week, which means no holiday. I'd keep using the chatbot to learn the robot side, the error codes and that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. But more like before an exam than before a car crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to watch someone else go first, which is how I like it. I'd see which robots break, which farms regret it, which jobs come out of it. Two years was a cliff, five is a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally fixing robots on farms round here, for a dealer or for the co-op. Leni and I would still be in Ashby, maybe with a bit saved. I wouldn't want kids until I knew I'd be working.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so let's use them to fund training and write the rules. At the co-op I'd ask for a plan, not just a vote on robots.
S3.think: Five years is enough to see who's doing it right and learn from the farms that go first. It still ends with most farm work gone, but I might keep the machines going for a while.
S3.do: Takes the evening machinery course and asks the co-op to pay half. Saves fifty a week by skipping holidays and uses a chatbot to learn robot error codes.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more like before an exam than before a crash.
S3.quote: Two years was a cliff, five is a steep hill.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Colin's style: he can watch others go first and then follow. He sets a clear target of repairing farm robots locally. He links having children to having secure work, which shows how much rides on the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so no one should be left behind, and if they are, that's a choice someone made. I'd be loud about that at the co-op and at elections. And I'd say farming will still need people for a while, so don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me ten years is good and bad. Good, because I'd have time to learn something solid. Bad, because I'd be 37 when it lands, which is old to start over, but at least it wouldn't be from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the college course properly and get a machinery certificate within two or three years. I'd save, slowly. I'd stay at Eastbrook and try to be the one who knows the new kit, because I'd have seen it work by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the background, but I could live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my weakness. I'd be waiting for proof, and proof might come just when everyone else rushes in. I'd have to set myself a date, like, by 2029 I'm qualified, no matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old who wanted to start on a farm now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but learn the machines as well as the animals. And join the union on day one, not when it's too late like me.

S4.say: We've got a decade, so if anyone gets left behind, that's a choice someone made. Farming will still need people for a while, so don't panic.
S4.think: Ten years gives me time to learn something solid, but I'd be 37 when it lands. That's old to start over, though at least not from nothing.
S4.do: Starts the college course and aims for a machinery certificate within two or three years, setting a 2029 deadline. Saves slowly and stays at Eastbrook as the person who knows the new kit.
S4.feel: Uneasy, in the background, but livable.
S4.quote: I'd have to set myself a date, like, by 2029 I'm qualified, no matter what.
S4.fieldNote: Colin knows his habit of waiting for proof could make him late, and answers it by setting himself a deadline. Ten years brings him down to uneasy because his plan fits his pace. His advice to a teenager, to learn machines and join a union on day one, sums up his outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole way of doing things is to wait and watch, and there'd be nothing to watch. What would help is a government income for people pushed out, and training paid for, not loans. And the co-op sharing whatever the robots save.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. If the co-op owns them, the savings stay in the village. If some company rents them to us, the money goes somewhere I'll never see.

headlineQuote: If some company rents them to us, the money goes somewhere I'll never see.
portrait: Colin Varga is 27, the junior hand in the pig unit at Eastbrook, a co-operative farm, and lives in Ashby with his partner Leni, a care assistant. He has about three weeks of rent saved and says one broken car would finish them. He uses a chatbot now and then but always checks with a person, and he only takes up something new once a neighbour has proven it. He stays calm in the plateau, grows anxious as robots arrive, and is alarmed by the two-year scenario because there'd be no one to watch first. With five or ten years he aims to qualify in farm machinery and wants the co-op, not a company, to own the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his way of coping is to wait and watch others first, and there would be no time for that.
whatWouldHelp: Government income for people pushed out of work, training paid for rather than loaned, and the co-op sharing what the robots save.
